text:
A: Hi, can you hear me alright?
B: Yes. I'm Abena.
A: Daniel. Nice to meet you. I'm in Worthing.
B: Thornton Heath, Croydon. What do you do, Daniel?
A: Erm, I run the trade counter at a builders' merchant in Lancing. Timber, plasterboard, quotes for builders. And you?
B: Practice administrator, at a GP surgery in Norbury.
A: Oh, really? My mum works on reception at a GP surgery. Part-time. In Worthing.
B: Then she knows eight o'clock.
A: [laughs] She does. She comes home some days and just sits in the kitchen for ten minutes not saying anything.
B: I understand that completely. The phones open, every line lights up, and the first person through has usually been waiting since five to eight and is already cross. Your mother deserves a medal, you know. Tell her somebody in Croydon said so.
A: I will. She'll like that.
B: Is she careful? With the records?
A: Erm, I think so. She's the one who keeps all our bills in a folder at home, so probably.
B: Good. Then she's useful.
A: [laughs] I'll pass that on as well.
B: You live with your parents?
A: Yeah. Moved back four years ago. I'm saving for a deposit. Thirty-two, so, erm, a bit behind, I sort of feel.
B: Behind whom?
A: I don't know, really. Everyone. Mates with houses, kids.
B: You pay rent?
A: Yeah.
B: You're saving?
A: Yeah.
B: Then you're not behind. You're being sensible. People who borrowed to look like they had everything at thirty, some of them are not doing so well now. I have seen it at church.
A: That's a fair way to put it. Thanks.
B: I noticed the books in your photo. You are studying?
A: Open University. Social history. I started a degree at eighteen and left after the first year, so I'm sort of having another go.
B: Why did you leave?
A: Money, mainly. And I was homesick, if I'm honest.
B: That's honest. I did a bookkeeping certificate at Croydon College in the evenings, after work. I already had an HND from Ghana, but here it didn't count for very much. So I did it again, the English way.
A: That must've been frustrating.
B: It was. But it's done. Do you finish your assignments on time?
A: Erm, mostly. One was a day late. I had a family thing.
B: Mostly is alright. One day is alright, if there was a reason.
A: [laughs] I feel like I'm being marked.
B: You're not. Not much.
A: What do you do to switch off, then?
B: I walk. Choir. My tomatoes. And I read crime novels, British police procedurals. Do you read those?
A: Not really. More history. Books about ordinary working lives, that kind of thing.
B: Then you would like some of the old ones. The detective is always the one who notices small things nobody else bothered—
